english.html: a basin full of water, where with certain charms one makes a spirit come, which at first quivers and leaps about in the water, and afterwards, hissing, utters a little voice, by which it answers what is asked of it <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. Geomancy is a divination which was practised of old, before the use of paper and ink had been found, by points cast on the earth; whence it took, and still keeps, its name; but now it is no longer practised on the earth, but on white paper or some other thing apt to receive the points and lines, from which the judgment is afterwards made. Chiromancy is divination made by inspection of the lines of the hand. Besides the aforesaid kinds of Magic, some set down another, which is called Pharmacy <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup> — wrongly, however, in my opinion, seeing that it does not consist solely in drugs, potions and poisonings, to make one die, or love, or else hate: as when, in the case of Faustina, daughter of Antoninus and wife of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher and Emperor, to make her lose the measureless love she bore to I know not what gladiator, for love of whom she was dying, [unclear: the print wants its main verb here — Capitolinus has the gladiator killed and Faustina bathed in his blood] and immediately after to lie with her husband; which she did, and so lost her love for that fine swordsman — true it is that she was that very hour got with child of Antoninus Commodus, a prince who was afterwards so cruel and bloodthirsty that he better deserved the name and title of gladiator than of Emperor or prince <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>. And although such potions are given for love, yet they are very dangerous, and from them there often follows either death or an extreme frenzy <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>: as in Lucretius (that great and excellent Poet), who, after eating what Lucilia his too-jealous wife had prepared for him, to draw him to her love, became so frenzied that he killed himself <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>. That is why Ovid strongly dissuades from the use of such love-charms, saying <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>:

notes.citation: Pietro Crinito, De honesta disciplina VI.11 (De Lecanomantia veterum)
notes.original: Pierre Crinit au vj. liu. de honeſta diſcipli. c. xj.

notes.citation: Lodovico Ricchieri (Cœle Rhodigin, Caelius Rhodiginus), Lectionum antiquarum libri IX.23 (as cited; chapter unverified)
notes.original: Cœle Rhodigin au liure ix. c. xxiij.
notes.gloss: Ricchieri of Rovigo, 1469–1525; his Antiquae lectiones (1516) treat the kinds of magic, among them pharmacia.

notes.citation: Julius Capitolinus, Life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher (Historia Augusta, Marcus 19.1–7)
notes.original: Iule Capitolin en la vie de M. Antonin philoſop.
notes.gloss: Faustina's passion for a gladiator; the Chaldeans advise that he be killed and she bathe in his blood and so lie with her husband; Commodus is conceived, and is reckoned a gladiator's son in spirit. This is the source that supplies the verb the print omits.

notes.citation: Digest 48.19.38.5 (De poenis, l. Si quis aliquid, § Qui abortionis, Paul)
notes.original: l. ſi quis aliquid P. qui abortionis. D. de pœn.
notes.gloss: Qui abortionis aut amatorium poculum dant, etsi dolo non faciant, tamen quia mali exempli res est…: those who give an abortifacient or a love-potion, even without evil intent, are punished, because the thing is of bad example — and if the person dies, with death. The print's P. is its sort for §.

notes.citation: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History VI as printed (the notice that Lucretius, driven mad by a love-philtre, killed himself is in Jerome's Latin continuation of Eusebius's Chronicle, under Ol. 171, not in the Ecclesiastical History); Jerome (Hiero.), "in the dissuasory against Rufinus" as printed (Jerome's Apology against Rufinus; the Lucretius passage has not been located there)
notes.original: Euſeb. Ceſarien. liure vj. de l'hiſto. eccleſi. Hiero. in diſſuaſorio contra Ruffinum.
notes.gloss: Jerome's Chronicle: T. Lucretius poeta nascitur, qui postea amatorio poculo in furorem versus … propria se manu interfecit. The wife's name Lucilia is a Renaissance addition, not Jerome's.

notes.citation: Ovid, Art of Love (Ars amatoria) 2.105–106 (the print cites "book II de Ponto", i.e. the Epistulae ex Ponto, where the lines are not)
notes.gloss: Nec data profuerint pallentia philtra puellis; / philtra nocent animis vimque furoris habent. The print's phyltra for philtra and habẽt for habent.

notes.original: Nec data profuerint, pallentia phyltra puellis. Phyltra nocent animis, vimque furoris habẽt.
notes.gloss: Two lines run together by the reflow; translated in the text with the Latin in parentheses.

english.html: Nor will pale philtres given to girls avail; philtres harm the mind, and carry the force of madness (Nec data profuerint pallentia philtra puellis; philtra nocent animis, vimque furoris habent).
I do not however wish to deny that, when from morsels or potions some prodigious effect should follow, Pharmacy might be placed among the
